overview.text: The human voice is the body’s sound-making instrument: air from the lungs passes through the larynx, where paired vocal folds vibrate to create sound. People use that sound for speech, singing, humming, cries, and other vocal expression. Voice is not identical to speech: it is the sound source, while coordinated movements of the tongue and lips shape it into recognizable speech sounds. The throat, mouth, and nose also modify the sound through resonance. The vocal folds and resonating spaces help determine pitch, volume, and tone, contributing to why voices differ. Because it can communicate words and carry melody, the voice is central to communication and music.

key_facts.text: The vocal folds are a pair of tissue bands in the larynx; they are open during quiet breathing and vibrate as air from the lungs passes them during voice production.
Voice is the sound source; speech forms recognizable sounds by coordinating movements of the tongue, lips, and other parts of the vocal tract.
The throat, mouth, and nose act as resonating spaces that modify vocal sound; their size and shape help influence voice quality.
Pitch, volume, and tone are among the qualities that help make voices sound different.
People use the voice for activities including speaking and singing, as well as vocal sounds such as humming and crying.
